summary.text: Take \(n=7\). Since the prescribed choices force \(x\ge 3\) and \(x\le y\le z\), any such triple would satisfy \(x+y+z\ge 3x\ge 9\), contradicting \(x+y+z=7\); hence the “moreover” assertion already fails, independently of the primality conditions.

full_proof.text:
Let \(a(n)\) denote the number of triples of positive integers \((x,y,z)\) satisfying
\[
x\le y\le z,\qquad x+y+z=n,
\]
for which all six integers
\[
2x-1,\quad 2y-1,\quad 2z-1,\quad 2xy-1,\quad 2xz-1,\quad 2yz-1
\]
are prime.

The conjecture is a conjunction of two assertions: first, that \(a(n)>0\) for every \(n>5\); and second, the stronger “moreover” assertion that whenever \(n>6\), there is such an ordered triple with
\[
x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\}.
\]
It suffices to disprove the second assertion, because if one clause of this conjunction is false, then the full conjecture is false.

Take
\[
n=7.
\]
Certainly \(7>6\), so the “moreover” assertion would require positive integers \(x,y,z\) such that
\[
x+y+z=7,\qquad x\le y\le z,
\]
with \(x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\}\), as well as the six stated primality conditions.

We show that even the elementary size and ordering conditions are impossible. Membership in the indicated finite set gives the five possible cases
\[
x=3,\quad x=4,\quad x=6,\quad x=10,\quad\text{or}\quad x=15.
\]
In every case, \(x\ge 3\). Since \(x\le y\), we also have \(y\ge x\ge 3\). Since \(y\le z\), we have \(z\ge y\ge x\ge 3\). Consequently,
\[
x+y+z\ge x+x+x=3x\ge 3\cdot 3=9.
\]
On the other hand, the required sum is \(x+y+z=7\). Combining these statements would give
\[
7=x+y+z\ge 9,
\]
which is impossible.

Thus no ordered positive triple summing to \(7\) can have its first entry in \(\{3,4,6,10,15\}\). In particular, no such triple can satisfy the additional primality requirements. Hence the “moreover” claim fails at \(n=7\), and therefore the combined conjecture about A229969 is false.
